title: Contrast connectors: sin embargo and no obstante

sections.content: You know *sin embargo* and *no obstante* from B1 Unit 1 (*no obstante* is the more formal one). They add a contrast with what was just said: something is true, but the result is surprising or different. Use them to show the paradox of the 1930s: countries rich in raw materials were still very vulnerable.

items.spanish: Los países vendían lo mismo; sin embargo, recibían mucho menos dinero.
items.english: The countries sold the same goods; however, they received much less money.

items.spanish: El gobierno quemó una parte del café. Sin embargo, el precio siguió bajo.
items.english: The government burned part of the coffee. However, the price stayed low.

items.spanish: Los países eran ricos en materias primas y, no obstante, eran muy vulnerables.
items.english: The countries were rich in raw materials and, nevertheless, they were very vulnerable.

items.spanish: Chile tenía muchas minas; no obstante, la crisis lo afectó más que a otros países.
items.english: Chile had many mines; nevertheless, the crisis affected it more than other countries.

sections.content: *Sin embargo* and *no obstante* usually start a new clause and take a comma after them. Put a full stop or a semicolon before them: *Vendían lo mismo; sin embargo, recibían menos.* They do not need *que*.
